newsitem.title: USA: New Alaska native hospital is dedicated.
newsitem.headline: New Alaska native hospital is dedicated.

text.p: The nation's biggest and most sophisticated hospital for native Americans was dedicated on Sunday with bands, balloons and dances.
The $168 million Alaska Native Medical Center -- a five-building complex in midtown Anchorage -- will open its doors June 2.

Officials said the new hospital helps fulfill the U.S. government's promise, made early this century, to provide lifetime health care for all native Americans in exchange for land taken from tribes and war damage inflicted on them.
Michael Trujillo, director of the Indian Health Service, said, "Many of our forefathers lost land, resources and their lives to bring about this type of facility and care."
"Let those who enter the doors of this facility always find caring. Let them be treated with dignity, respect and honesty," said Trujillo, a Laguna Pueblo Indian from New Mexico.

The new center replaces an old downtown Alaska Native hospital that opened in 1953 as a tuberculosis sanitarium. By that year, one in 10 native Alaskans was stricken with tuberculosis, and one in 30 was eventually hospitalized for the disease, said David Schraer, acting area director for the Alaska Native Health Service.

In the early days of the old hospital, doctors answered health queries from outlying rural villages that came in by mail, telephone -- if it existed in the villages -- and radio, said Gov. Tony Knowles.

The Democratic governor lauded the progress of medical care for Alaska Natives, which he said advanced "from the weeks taken to deliver serum on the Iditarod Trail (in 1925) to the instantaneous tele-medicine this facility will provide."
